title: Closed-Form Optimal Weight Splitting for Matrix–Vector Multiply on Noisy In-Memory Accelerators
venue: arXiv:2610.20359v1 [cs.ET], 14 Oct 2026 (workshop paper on low-precision hardware, per the intro's wording; venue not named)
whatRead: Full text of the arXiv HTML version (v1), including the main body, Table I, figure captions, the scope-and-limitations paragraph and the reference list. Figure images themselves were not seen, only their captions. No appendix, code or supplementary material appeared in the source. Cited papers were not opened.
verdict: The paper adds a uniform-quantization floor to the equal-fill slicing-noise term of Le Gallo et al. and obtains a closed-form interior optimal base, b_opt = 1 + 1/(12 bound² η²). The derivation is short and internally consistent, and the simulator sweep shows an inverted-U peaking at b=5. However, η is calibrated by reading the peak location of that same sweep, so the 'prediction' in the device-physics test is partly circular, and the headline +3.3 dB is measured against a non-overlapping base-16 baseline that the paper itself shows leaves gaps in the grid. Useful as a design rule for additive-noise-limited tiles; weaker as evidence for real hardware.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
The paper asks how to split each weight across several noisy multi-level cells in an analog in-memory crossbar so that the summed MVM output has minimum error. The authors describe a tension. A large base b gives a fine reconstruction grid but multiplies the high tile's noise by its place value b. A base near one averages the noise, as in duplication, but adds no resolution. They say the closest prior analysis (Le Gallo et al.) models only noise. That term is monotone in b, so it always selects b=1 (equal-fill). Other work fixes the base empirically or searches for it (Mackin et al. use evolutionary search and report a value of two; Diware et al. split bits empirically). The stated gap is a model that carries both noise and the finite-grid quantization floor, so that a nontrivial base can be read off from one device-noise measurement instead of being searched.

My read: the motivation is reasonably convincing as a design-knob question, and the 'monotone in b implies b=1' observation is a clean setup. It is narrower than the intro suggests, though. It holds only if the dominant output noise is additive, and the paper itself says real PCM noise is state-dependent (multiplicative), which is the regime where b=1 is already optimal. How often the additive regime is the relevant one is asserted, not shown.

sections.title: Core idea
sections.content: Each weight is stored as n_W integer cell states s_k in [-bound, bound] (bound = 2^(q-1) - 1; 7 for signed 4-bit) and decoded by a place-value sum: [ \hat{w} = \mathrm{scale}\cdot\sum_{k=0}^{n_W-1} b^{k} s_k . ] b=1 is equal-fill, b=2^q is a non-overlapping bit-slice, and intermediate integer b is the 'overlap' regime. For n_W=2 the weight is master-quantized onto a grid of range bound(1+b), then split as (m=\mathrm{round}(w/\mathrm{scale})), (s_H=\mathrm{trunc}(m/b)), (s_L=m-b s_H), with (\mathrm{scale}=W_{\max}/[\mathrm{bound}(1+b)]). The grid has no gaps only for (b\le 2\,\mathrm{bound}+1), and the low digit stays unsaturated for (b\le \mathrm{bound}+1); the paper uses the latter as its validity range. The noise model assumes each tile read adds independent additive Gaussian error (n_k\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\rm out}^2)) that does not scale with the stored code. Place-value scaling is applied after the noisy read, so output noise variance is [ \mathrm{Var}(\hat y)_{\rm noise}=\mathrm{scale}^2\sigma_{\rm out}^2(1+b^2). ] Under i.i.d. Gaussian weights and inputs, clipping at (k_\sigma=3), and (\Delta=\mathrm{scale}), adding the uniform-quantization term (\Delta^2/12) gives [ \mathrm{relMSE}(b)=k_\sigma^2\eta^2\frac{1+b^2}{(1+b)^2}+\frac{k_\sigma^2}{12\,\mathrm{bound}^2(1+b)^2}. ] Setting the derivative to zero yields [ b_{\rm opt}=1+\frac{1}{12\,\mathrm{bound}^2\eta^2}\quad(\text{capped at }2\,\mathrm{bound}+1). ] η is the per-tile output-noise std relative to per-tile signal RMS. As η→0 the optimum goes to the cap (pure bit-slicing), and as η→∞ it goes to 1 (duplication). For general n_W the noise factor becomes T/S² with (S=(b^{n_W}-1)/(b-1)) and (T=(b^{2n_W}-1)/(b^2-1)), and the paper reports numerically that the best integer base falls from 5 (n_W=2) to 2 (n_W=3,4) at η=0.02. A fixed block-diagonal random orthogonal rotation of W, shared across tiles and cancelled in the product, is used to push operands toward Gaussian. My read: the derivation as written is straightforward and the algebra is consistent with what the paper states. I did not check it independently. Two things matter for use. First, the formula takes the integer b as a continuous variable and rounds afterwards; the paper argues the minimum is shallow enough that this is harmless. Second, the key modeling step is that quantization and noise both scale as 1/(1+b)² after normalization, so only the numerator of the noise term grows with b. The interior optimum exists only because of that additive-noise assumption.

sections.title: Distinguishing factor
sections.content:
vs. Le Gallo et al. (closed-form slicing error, PCM chip): the paper says its noise term is algebraically identical to their equal-fill expression and adds only the quantization floor. Their model is noise-only and monotone in b, giving b=1; the paper reframes that as the noise-dominated limit of its formula. They note an interior b=2 case in Le Gallo et al. that came from an error-correction programming algorithm, not the representation. So the novelty is one added term plus the observation that under additive noise it moves the optimum. It is small in mathematical content but changes the conclusion.

vs. empirical or searched bases (Mackin et al., Diware et al.): these fix or search the base per device or model. The paper offers a closed form from one η measurement. Caveat: η is not a datasheet constant. The paper says it aggregates programming noise, IR-drop, ADC quantization, normalization and operand distribution, and it was obtained in the experiments by inverting the simulator's peak location, so the 'search-free' claim in practice means a one-parameter fit that still requires a base sweep (or an equivalent noise measurement the paper does not demonstrate).

vs. the 64-core PCM chip paper: cited for the error decomposition and as the b=1 corner; no head-to-head.

vs. low-precision numerics and rotation-based quantization (QuIP#, SpinQuant): used only as framing and as the 'rotated non-uniform' baseline. The paper says its contribution is orthogonal (multi-cell significance base versus within-cell codebook).

vs. their earlier version: the paper does not mention one, so no comparison applies.

My read: the distinguishing step is real but modest. It is closer to a corrected modeling assumption than a new method, and whether it matters depends on which noise regime a given device is in.

sections.title: Evaluation and conclusions
sections.content: Three fidelity levels are used: Monte-Carlo, a device-physics simulator, and end applications. Monte-Carlo check. Sweeping the base for η in {0.02, 0.05, 0.10}, relative MSE from Monte-Carlo tracks the closed form within about 1% for b ≤ bound+1, with SNR peaks at the predicted b_opt = {5.25, 1.68, 1.17}. My read: this confirms that the algebra matches a simulation of the same model; it does not test the model's assumptions. It is a sanity check, not evidence about hardware. Device-physics simulation. A 512×512 array of signed 4-bit differential cells with programming variation, IR-drop and ADC quantization, run on layers of Gemma-3 270M and Llama-3.2 1B. Mean per-layer SNR peaks at b=5, about 1.6 dB above b=1 and about 3.3–3.4 dB above base-16, with a flat top at b=3–8. The authors then invert the peak (b=5) through the formula to get η≈0.02. My read: the inverted-U shape and the fact that it survives non-additive effects is the most informative result. But recovering η from the peak and then calling the formula predictive is partly circular, and the paper says nothing was sampled between b=8 and b=16, so the base-16 comparison is a single separated point. Also, base-16 already violates the paper's own validity bound (16 > 15), so the 3.3 dB figure compares against a configuration with representable-grid gaps, which a practitioner would likely avoid. The simulator is the authors' own, so it shows consistency with their model rather than with silicon. Per-tile consistency. 48% of Gemma tiles and 46% of Llama tiles peak at b=5, and 92% and 97% fall within b in {4,5,6}; per-tile base sensitivity is 0.22 dB. My read: this supports a single global base within this simulator and these two models, helped by the rotation. It does not show the same for other devices. End-application accuracy. On a 2D Laplacian and an ill-conditioned dense matrix (κ=10³), the same inverted-U appears, peaking at b≈4–6 with about 3.4 dB over base-16. On eight zero-shot tasks (ten-run means, ±0.008 run-to-run noise), base-N at b=6 gives +13.1% (Gemma) and +9.0% (Llama) relative to equal-fill, versus +12.3% and +7.7% for residual redundancy and +4.6% and +3.9% for rotated non-uniform. Equal-fill is the worst row. Re-running at b=5 changes accuracy by +0.0003 (Gemma) and −0.006 (Llama). My read: base-N is better than equal-fill and rotated non-uniform; against residual redundancy the gap is within noise, as the paper itself says. Table I reports only relative percentage change, so absolute accuracy is hidden, and the baselines are simulated in the same noise model. Surprising item: the 'rotated non-uniform' baseline is much weaker than residual redundancy, despite using the same rotation the method relies on for homogenization. Conclusion in the paper: equal-fill is optimal only for multiplicative noise; under additive noise the best base is interior, determined by η and cell resolution, and the base can be set before programming from one η measurement. My read: partly supported. The interior optimum under additive noise is supported within the authors' model and simulator. The 'determined before programming from one measurement' claim is not demonstrated, since η was fitted from the sweep. The reach to real devices is untested, and the paper concedes mixed noise would pull the optimum back toward b=1.
results: Monte-Carlo vs closed form: agreement within about 1% for b ≤ bound+1, SNR peaks at predicted b_opt = 5.25, 1.68, 1.17 for η = 0.02, 0.05, 0.10 (checks the algebra against the same model, not hardware).

Device-physics simulator (Gemma-3 270M, Llama-3.2 1B): inverted-U SNR peaking at b=5, about 1.6 dB over b=1 and about 3.3–3.4 dB over base-16; flat top at b=3–8; η≈0.02 obtained by inverting the peak.
Per-tile optimum: 92–97% of tiles peak within b in {4,5,6}; correlations of best base with weight std, kurtosis and dynamic range all |r|<0.05.

Eight-task transformer accuracy relative to equal-fill: base-N (b=6) +13.1% Gemma and +9.0% Llama, residual redundancy +12.3% and +7.7%, rotated non-uniform +4.6% and +3.9%; base-N vs residual redundancy is within the ±0.008 noise.
Laplacian single matvec: about +1.6 dB over b=1 at b=6, peak at b≈4–6 and about 3.4 dB over base-16.
sections.conclusion: The paper concludes that, under additive tile-output noise, the best base is interior and set by η and cell resolution, reversing the equal-fill guidance. The evidence supports this inside the authors' model and simulator; it does not establish it on real devices, and the η calibration is not independent of the sweep.

entries.text: The base must be an integer, because s_L = m − b·s_H is integral only then; b_opt is a continuous relaxation that is rounded afterwards. The two-cell construction is only valid up to b ≤ bound+1 (7+1 = 8 for 4-bit cells), and the paper's own base-16 reference lies outside that range, with unreachable grid values such as ±8.

The Gaussian-operand assumption is enforced in practice by a fixed block-diagonal random orthogonal rotation shared across tiles and seeded, with one extra matmul per tile block. The paper credits the same rotation with making all tiles prefer nearly the same base, so a single global base works. The 'rotated non-uniform' baseline uses the same rotation, so the gain over it is not due to rotation.

η is not a datasheet number. The paper says it aggregates programming noise, IR-drop, ADC quantization, normalization and operand distribution. In the experiments it is obtained by inverting the simulator's peak (b=5 gives η≈0.02), which makes the 'one measurement' calibration an inference from a sweep rather than an independent measurement.

The closed-form derivation uses a common σ_out for the high and low tiles; the device sweep uses true per-tile noise. The paper treats the mismatch as a relaxation, but it is never quantified separately.

For n_W>2 the paper reports numerically that the best integer base drops from 5 (n_W=2) to 2 (n_W=3,4) at η=0.02. All end-application results use n_W=2, so the larger-cell regime has no end-to-end validation.

Table I reports everything relative to equal-fill and hides absolute accuracy and SNR levels; the Laplacian rows for the two neural-network baselines are omitted as having no fixed scientific-matvec analog.

rows.question: Fair comparison to external baselines?
rows.answer: Partly. On accuracy it compares against equal-fill, rotated non-uniform and residual redundancy at the same two-cell budget, with ten-run means. But the headline SNR gain is against non-overlapping base-16, which the paper itself shows has grid gaps, and the baselines are run in the authors' own simulated noise model. Evolutionary-search weight programming (Mackin et al.) and unbalanced bit-slicing (Diware et al.) are discussed but not run as baselines, and no real-chip result is shown.

rows.question: Invents its own FoM?
rows.answer: Mostly no. It uses relative MVM MSE / SNR and eight-task zero-shot accuracy, which are standard. The custom parts are η, defined as per-tile noise std over signal RMS and fitted from the sweep, and results given only relative to b=1, with absolute levels withheld.

rows.question: Rewrite of an existing idea?
rows.answer: Partly. The noise term is, by the paper's own statement, identical to the equal-fill slicing error of Le Gallo et al. (their Eq. 8). The addition is the Δ²/12 quantization floor and the resulting interior optimum under additive noise. The overlapping place-value split also echoes unbalanced bit-slicing and Mackin's unequal significance factor. The novelty is the closed form and regime analysis, not the encoding family.

rows.question: Reliable enough to reuse?
rows.answer: As a design heuristic for additive-noise-dominated tiles, yes: the formula is simple and the optimum is flat (b=3–8). As a drop-in calibration rule, not yet: η must still be extracted from sweeps or measurements the paper does not demonstrate, real crossbars have mixed noise that pulls the optimum toward 1 (acknowledged but unquantified), results rest on the authors' simulator and two small models, and n_W>2 and iterative solvers are untested.

sections.title: Sources and limits
sections.content: I read the full arXiv HTML text (v1), including the main body, the scope-and-limitations paragraph, Table I and the reference list. I did not see the figure images, any appendix, code or supplementary data; the paper's text mentions none. I did not check the derivations, arithmetic or cross-table numbers, and I did not open any cited paper. Claims about the simulator (its code, parameters, per-layer sampling) could not be verified from the text, and the exact experimental protocol for η calibration is not described beyond inverting the peak location. Citations below are only papers named in the source text.
